extracted.intended_audience: graduate/advanced-undergraduate students in algebraic geometry (Math 216; readers of Vakil's Foundations)
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-level textbook guidance and definitions for basic scheme theory: Noetherian rings/modules, Hilbert Basis Theorem, the correspondence V↔I, the structure sheaf, and the definition/properties of schemes with worked examples and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian ring (ascending chain condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring is Noetherian if every ascending sequence of ideals eventually stabilizes: there is an r such that I_r = I_{r+1} = ··· (the ascending chain condition on ideals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently (Exercise 3.6.Q), every ideal of A is finitely generated. Quick facts: fields and Z are Noetherian; images of Noetherian rings under ring homomorphisms (quotients) are Noetherian; localizations S^{-1}A are Noetherian; polynomial rings over Noetherian rings are Noetherian (Hilbert Basis Theorem). Counterexamples: k[x1,x2,...] is not Noetherian (strictly ascending chains like (x1) ⊂ (x1,x2) ⊂ ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian module (ACC on submodules)
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-module is Noetherian if it satisfies the ascending chain condition for submodules (every ascending chain of submodules stabilizes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ring A is Noetherian iff it is a Noetherian A-module. Consequences/exercises: submodules of Noetherian modules are finitely generated (3.6.U); in a short exact sequence 0→M'→M→M''→0, M is Noetherian iff M' and M'' are (3.6.V); A^⊕n is Noetherian when A is (3.6.W); finitely generated modules over Noetherian rings are Noetherian (3.6.X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert Basis Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is Noetherian, then A[x] is Noetherian (Theorem 3.6.17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: given ideal I ⊂ A[x], choose generators f1,f2,... inductively by minimal degree; consider leading coefficients a_n in A. Since A is Noetherian the ideal generated by the a_n stabilizes; produce a relation expressing a_{N+1} in terms of previous a_i and construct a linear combination of earlier f_i to contradict minimality unless the process terminates. Consequence: polynomial rings over fields or Z and their quotients/localizations are Noetherian; most 'nice' rings encountered are Noetherian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spec A Noetherian topological space iff A Noetherian (one direction)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is Noetherian, then Spec A is a Noetherian topological space (Exercise 3.6.S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note converse fails: Spec A can be Noetherian as a topological space while A is not Noetherian (example: A = k[x1,x2,x3,...]/(x1,x2,x3,...) where Spec A has one point). Use this to understand geometric vs. algebraic Noetherian notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: I(S): ideal of functions vanishing on a subset S
rubrics_metrics.description: For a subset S ⊂ Spec A, define I(S) to be the set of functions in A vanishing on every point of S (equivalently intersection of primes in S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations: I(S) is an ideal; I(S) is inclusion-reversing (S1 ⊂ S2 ⇒ I(S2) ⊂ I(S1)); I(S) is always a radical ideal. Exercises include computing generators for concrete S ⊂ Spec k[x,y] (3.7.A, 3.7.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: V(I) and I(V): correspondence between closed subsets and radical ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: V(·) and I(·) give an inclusion-reversing bijection between closed subsets of Spec A and radical ideals of A (Theorem 3.7.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: V(I(S)) = closure of S; for an ideal J, I(V(J)) = √J (Exercise 3.7.D). This is the scheme-theoretic basis of the geometric–algebraic dictionary (sometimes called Nullstellensatz in special cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreducible closed subsets ↔ prime ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: V(·) gives a bijection between irreducible closed subsets of Spec A and prime ideals of A; hence points correspond to irreducible closed subsets with unique generic point (Exercise 3.7.E/3.7.F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to identify minimal primes with irreducible components; deduce that Noetherian rings have finitely many minimal primes (via Proposition 3.6.15 and related exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the structure sheaf O_{Spec A} on distinguished opens
rubrics_metrics.description: For a distinguished open D(f) ⊂ Spec A, define O_{Spec A}(D(f)) to be the localization A_f at the multiplicative set of functions that do not vanish outside V(f) (i.e., those g with V(g) ⊂ V(f)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This depends only on D(f), not the choice of f. Define restriction maps between distinguished opens by further localizations. Theorem 4.1.2: these data define a sheaf on the distinguished base and hence a sheaf on Spec A (the structure sheaf).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaf axioms on the distinguished base (base identity and base gluability)
rubrics_metrics.description: To verify O_{Spec A} is a sheaf reduce to verifying base identity (injectivity on sections) and base gluability (exactness/ability to glue compatible local sections) on distinguished opens; concretely this is encoded in an equalizer/exact sequence like 0 → A → ∏_i A_{f_i} → ∏_{i≠j} A_{f_if_j}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses quasicompactness (finite subcovers) and a 'partition of unity' argument: if Spec A = ⋃ D(f_i) with a finite subcover, there exist r_i with Σ r_i f_i^m = 1 allowing lifting/gluing of local sections. Finite vs infinite index set handled by reduction to finite case via base identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaf associated to an A-module M (quasi-coherent module proto-construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an A-module M define M(D(f)) to be the localization M_f; with analogous restriction maps this defines a sheaf of O_{Spec A}-modules on the distinguished base (Exercise/Definition 4.1.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One obtains an exact sequence 0 → M → ∏ M_{f_i} → ∏ M_{f_if_j} analogous to the structure sheaf case. This identifies M with a submodule of a product of localizations (useful for affine communication lemmas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexample: sections over arbitrary open U are not just localization at functions nonvanishing on U
rubrics_metrics.description: It is false in general that O_{Spec A}(U) equals the localization of A at the multiplicative set of functions not vanishing on U (4.1.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexample: two copies of A^2 glued at origins; the function that's 1 on one copy minus origin and 0 on the other is a section on U but not of that localization form. Be cautious: the distinguished base construction is sufficient to define the sheaf but naïve global-local localization description can fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization of nonreduced schemes (nilpotents) via 'fuzz'
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotients by nonradical ideals (e.g., A/(x^2)) should be pictured as the underlying closed set with infinitesimal 'fuzz' carrying derivative-order information: C[x]/(x^2) is the origin with first-order infinitesimal fuzz, C[x]/(x^3) has more fuzz, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (x,y)^2 in C[x,y] is a circular fuzz (first derivatives in all directions); (x^2,y) is fuzz only in x-direction; intersections of ideals correspond to intersections of fuzzed pictures. Use these pictures to understand scheme-theoretic intersections and multiplicity (e.g., parabola y=x^2 ∩ x-axis gives Spec C[x,y]/(y,x^2)). Associated points and location of fuzz are made precise later (5.5, 13.7.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of scheme and isomorphisms of ringed spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A ringed space (X, O_X) is an affine scheme if it is isomorphic to (Spec A, O_{Spec A}) for some A. A scheme is a ringed space such that every point has a neighborhood isomorphic to an affine scheme. An isomorphism of ringed spaces is a homeomorphism of underlying spaces together with an isomorphism of sheaves (pullback/pushforward via the homeomorphism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: Γ(X,O_X) recovers A for an affine scheme; identifications of distinguished opens D(f) with Spec A_f give compatibility of topology and sheaf; exercises explore uniqueness of the ring from Spec and functorial identifications (4.3.A, 4.3.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stalks and residue fields: value at a point
rubrics_metrics.description: The stalk of O_{Spec A} at the point [p] is the local ring A_p; the residue field κ(p) = A_p / p A_p is the value field at that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: sections are determined by germs; an A-module M is zero iff all localizations M_p are zero. Localization at p and quotient by p commute (A_p / pA_p = K(A/p)). The fiber of an O_X-module F at p is F_p ⊗_{O_{X,p}} κ(p) (4.3.7). Exercises: show invertibility and vanishing loci properties using stalks (4.3.G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally ringed space condition
rubrics_metrics.description: A ringed space is locally ringed if all its stalks are local rings (Definition 4.3.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schemes are locally ringed spaces (stalks are A_p). Interpreting quotient by maximal ideal as evaluation at a point gives geometric intuition for vanishing and invertibility of functions; use this to reason about where sections vanish or are units (4.3.G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete computation example: functions on A^2 minus origin and non-affineness
rubrics_metrics.description: For A = k[x,y], U = A^2_k − {(0,0)} = D(x) ∪ D(y). The global sections Γ(U, O_{A^2}) equal k[x,y] (Ax ∩ Ay = k[x,y]). Despite being a scheme, U is not affine: if U were Spec A' then Γ(U,O)=A' would equal k[x,y], and the missing point (x,y) would still correspond to a prime, contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This example illustrates computing sections by gluing on distinguished opens and shows that removing a codimension-2 point does not produce new global regular functions (analogy with Hartogs phenomenon). It provides a canonical counterexample when seeking non-affine schemes.
